items.title: How big should a parliament be?
items.headline: The Union Cabinet approved a plan to raise every state's Lok Sabha seats by half
items.news: On Friday, 27 November 2026, the Union Cabinet approved a plan to raise every state's Lok Sabha seats by the same 50%, news reports said, so Uttar Pradesh would go from 80 to 120 and Bihar from 40 to 60. The House would grow from 543 to about 815 seats, and each state's share, based on the 1971 census, would stay frozen until 2051. The plan is linked to starting the 2023 law that keeps a third of seats for women. Parliament was called for a special sitting from 30 November to 3 December; the bill has not been passed, and as a change to the Constitution it needs two-thirds of members voting in each House. An earlier version failed in April 2026 with 298 votes when 352 were needed, and DMK chief M.K. Stalin had said Tamil Nadu's 7.18% share must not fall. This entry explains why a country might grow its parliament, and what it gains and gives up.
items.hook: A British MP speaks for about 1 lakh people. With 543 seats, an Indian MP in the Lok Sabha speaks for more than 25 lakh. So how many MPs is right?

items.title: Why put warning labels on junk food?
items.headline: Supreme Court orders warnings on packaged foods high in fat, sugar or salt
items.news: On Thursday 26 November 2026, Constitution Day, Supreme Court Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran ordered the food regulator FSSAI to require front-of-pack warnings on packaged foods high in fat, sugar or salt, in a case brought by the health group 3S and Our Health Society. Each warning must be a separate hexagon reading "High Fat", "High Sugar" or "High Salt", covering at least about 4 to 5% of the front of the pack. The limits must count total sugars and saturated fat, rest on evidence and be "neither too low nor too high", and FSSAI must draw up a full list of exempt foods with reasons. FSSAI has about four months to draw up the rules, with 60 days for public comments, and companies then get 365 days to change their packets. ThePrint reported the court as saying that a consumer in India is entitled to "no less protection, and no less information" than one in the United States or the United Kingdom. This entry explains how warning labels work and why countries argue about them.
items.hook: In Chile, a small black stop sign on snack packets changed what went inside the packets, as well as what people bought.

items.title: Can a country make too much?
items.headline: The US proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods over "excess capacity"
items.news: On 25 November 2026, the office of the US Trade Representative announced the results of investigations it began in March 2026. It said 14 of the 16 economies it had looked at, including India, China, the European Union and Japan, have practices that create "structural excess capacity" in manufacturing, naming sectors such as steel, solar and medicines for India. It proposed an extra tariff of up to 25% on most Indian goods, which would be lowered to 17% if India signs a trade deal with the US. This is only a proposal, with written comments due by 5 January 2027 and public hearings from 25 January 2027. India's Department of Commerce said India "does not have structural excess capacity in any sector", that the notice was under examination, and that trade concerns should be settled in the trade deal it is negotiating with the US. This entry explains what overcapacity means and why countries argue over it.
items.hook: When a market is flooded with mangoes, prices crash and some farmers lose money. The same thing can happen with steel, solar panels and cars, but across the whole world.

items.title: Why are so many Indians anaemic?
items.headline: A huge national blood survey finds less anaemia in India than earlier counts
items.news: On Monday 23 November 2026, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) released the anaemia results of SAMPADA, a nutrition survey carried out from 2023 to 2025 that ICMR called one of the largest in the world. It covered more than 2 lakh people in over 81,000 homes, across 183 districts in 35 states and Union Territories. It found anaemia in about 42% of young children aged 1 to 4, 46% of girls aged 10 to 19 and 56% of women of child-bearing age. About half of these cases were mild, and severe anaemia was below 2% in most age groups. The figures were lower than earlier national surveys, which tested a drop of blood from a finger, while SAMPADA took blood from a vein and tested it with lab machines. This entry explains what anaemia is and why so many Indians have it.
items.hook: Every red blood cell carries tiny specks of iron. When there are too few, you feel tired and breathless, and millions of Indians do.

items.title: What does a company's board do?
items.headline: Nvidia's board reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive, and its shares jump
items.news: On Monday 23 November 2026, the board of Nvidia, the American company whose chips power much of the world's artificial intelligence, voted unanimously to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive. Huang had resigned on 12 November after, NPR reported, telling the board about personal behaviour that went against the company's code of conduct. On 17 November the board's chair, Harvey Jones, said it did not intend to bring him back. The board said a committee of independent directors was still investigating reports about Huang, and that Colette Kress, interim chief executive since his exit, would carry on as finance chief. Reuters reported that his return followed pressure from US President Donald Trump, and that Nvidia's shares rose more than 31% before the US market opened, lifting other chip shares. This entry explains what a company's board is and how it can remove, and bring back, even a founder.
items.hook: Even the person who started a company can lose their job there. A small group called the board has the power to hire and fire the boss.

items.title: Why can't we quit fossil fuels?
items.headline: UN climate summit COP31 ends without its main deal after a fight over fossil fuels
items.news: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on Sunday 22 November 2026 without adopting its main agreement, after two days of overtime. COP31 President Murat Kurum said: "I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted." The European Union objected because the final text left out any mention of fossil fuels, and Panama and the Marshall Islands also refused to back it. An early draft from Australia, which led the talks, had called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a later draft dropped every mention after Saudi Arabia and other oil and gas producers objected. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said: "There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science." This entry explains why the world finds it so hard to agree on giving up coal, oil and gas.
items.hook: Coal, oil and gas still give the world about four of every five units of its energy. Giving them up means some countries giving up their biggest earner.

items.title: Why do superpower meetings matter?
items.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin held their first three-way meeting and issued a joint statement on nuclear risks
items.news: On Thursday 19 November 2026, US President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin met for about an hour and a half in Shenzhen, China. It was the first meeting of just these three leaders, held beside the summit of APEC, a group of 21 Pacific economies. Their joint statement, released by Russia and China and shared by the White House, said a nuclear war cannot be won and promised talks on cutting nuclear risks. They also agreed to raise oil and fuel supplies, back reform of the United Nations and warn the International Criminal Court not to abuse its powers. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty called it a historic meeting with few concrete commitments, noting that the statement did not name the Iran war and that Ukraine was not on the agenda. India is not an APEC member and was not part of the meeting; this entry explains what such meetings can and cannot do.
items.hook: When the leaders of the world's most powerful countries sit at one table, everyone else watches. Sometimes a handshake changes history. Often, nothing much happens at all.

items.title: What is genocide?
items.headline: The world's top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
items.news: On Thursday 19 November 2026, the International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya people during army operations in Rakhine State in 2017. The judges decided nine votes to six, in a case The Gambia brought in 2019 under the Genocide Convention. It was the first time the court had found a country itself responsible for genocide. The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and prosecute those suspected, to make the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees possible, and to report back within two years on repairing the harm. Myanmar had long denied genocide, saying its forces were responding to attacks by an armed group. The ruling was final and could not be appealed. This entry explains how such a case works, from the first application to the final vote.
items.hook: The world's top court has no army, no police and no jail. Yet countries send their best lawyers to The Hague to argue in front of it.

items.title: How do scientists know where a cyclone will hit?
items.headline: Cyclone Akvan was forecast to cross the Odisha–Andhra coast; tens of thousands moved to safety
items.news: On 19 November 2026, the India Meteorological Department said Severe Cyclonic Storm Akvan, over the west-central Bay of Bengal, was expected to bring winds of 90–100 km/h gusting to 110 km/h. It forecast that Akvan would cross the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coast between Narsapur and Puri, close to Gopalpur, on Friday 20 November. Odisha moved tens of thousands of people from risky areas, including landslide-prone hills, to shelters; reports of the total ranged from about 72,000 to more than 1 lakh. Schools and anganwadi centres in six Odisha districts were shut from 19 to 21 November. The storm had not yet reached land when this entry was written. This entry explains how forecasters work out where and when a cyclone will reach the coast, days before it gets there.
items.hook: A cyclone far out at sea cannot be seen from any beach. Yet forecasters can often name the stretch of coast it will cross, days before it arrives.

items.title: Why are the USA and Iran fighting?
items.headline: Iran strikes at a US air base in Kuwait and at Bahrain, as tankers with Indian crews are hit near Hormuz
items.news: On 17 November 2026, a US fighter jet struck a missile launch site of Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, after Iran attacked a US radar in Bahrain earlier that day. Early on 18 November, Iran targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, which US forces use, and launched several attacks on Bahrain, home to the US Navy's 5th Fleet; both countries said their air defences intercepted the attacks. On 16 November, the gas tanker Tara Gas, with 24 Indian sailors on board, was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, in what Indian officials called a missile attack; 21 were taken safely to Khasab in Oman, two went to hospital and one was missing. On 18 November, another tanker, Navig8 Messi, with three Indians on board, was hit near Hormuz, and India's shipping minister said all its crew were safe. India's Ministry of External Affairs called the attacks on ships "deeply worrisome" and asked for them to stop. This entry explains how a quarrel that began more than 70 years ago turned into this war.
items.hook: For about 25 years after 1953, the USA and Iran were close friends. Since 1979 they have been rivals, and in 2026 that rivalry became a war that reached Indian kitchens, airports and ships.

items.title: What makes a great captain?
items.headline: MS Dhoni retires from the IPL and becomes Chennai Super Kings' team mentor
items.news: On Tuesday 17 November 2026, it was announced that MS Dhoni had retired as a player from the Indian Premier League. He will stay with Chennai Super Kings as the team's mentor from the 2027 season. The news came on the day IPL teams had to name the players they were keeping for 2027. Dhoni, now 45, first played for Chennai in the very first IPL season in 2008, captained them to five titles, and did not play in the 2026 season. He retired from international cricket in August 2020. This entry explains the skill his career is most remembered for, leading a team under pressure.
items.hook: A captain cannot bat for everyone or bowl every ball. Yet one quiet decision, like who bowls the last over, can win or lose a World Cup.

items.title: How does a film make money at the box office?
items.headline: Ramayana: Part 1 sells more than 1,200 crore rupees of tickets worldwide in its first ten days
items.news: Ramayana, a big-budget film of the ancient epic directed by Nitesh Tiwari, with Ranbir Kapoor as Ram and Yash as Ravana, opened in cinemas on 5 November 2026, in the week of Diwali. Its makers planned a release on about 59,000 screens around the world. On Monday 9 November, early estimates from the tracking site Sacnilk said it earned more in India than any Indian film had ever earned on a first Monday. By its tenth day, trade trackers estimated it had made more than 1,200 crore rupees worldwide, about 820 crore of it in India and the rest abroad. These are estimates from the film trade, not official figures. This entry explains what those big box office numbers really count, and how much of the money a film's makers actually get.
items.hook: When a headline says a film "made 1,000 crore", that money does not land in one pocket. The government, the cinema and the film's makers all take a piece, and the makers usually get well under half.

items.title: How can a company lose a trillion dollars in a week?
items.headline: Nvidia says Jensen Huang has stepped down as its boss, and finance chief Colette Kress is leading it for now
items.news: On 12 November 2026, Nvidia, the American company whose chips power much of the world's artificial intelligence, said its co-founder Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive and left its board, with immediate effect, giving no reason. US news reports linked his exit to a board investigation, still unfinished, into reports about his private life and whether a foreign spy had targeted him; The Wall Street Journal had reported that the board was preparing to remove him. Colette Kress, the company's finance chief, now leads Nvidia as interim chief executive while the board looks for a permanent one. News reports said Nvidia was worth about 5.8 trillion dollars at its record in early October, and about 3.9 trillion dollars by 13 November, partly because AI shares were falling everywhere. Nvidia reports its results for the latest three months on 17 November. This entry explains how a company's value can rise and fall so fast.
items.hook: In 2026, the chipmaker Nvidia was worth more than every company on India's stock market put together. Within weeks, more than a trillion dollars of that value vanished, yet the company still had its factories, its chips and its customers.

items.title: Why does the narrow Strait of Hormuz matter so much to the world?
items.headline: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three oil tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz
items.news: On 14 November 2026, Iran's state news agency IRNA quoted the navy of Iran's Revolutionary Guards as saying three oil tankers caught fire after hitting sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz. It said the ships were trying to use a route Iran has banned. Reuters said it could not check the claim. A day earlier, the Revolutionary Guard said it had struck a US early warning radar in Bahrain. The US military said this was not true. It said it shot down two Iranian drones flying towards Bahrain, and that nothing was damaged and no one was hurt. Far fewer ships than normal have used the strait since the USA and Israel began strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026 and Iran hit back. A barrel of Brent crude cost about 96 dollars in mid-November, against about 73 dollars just before the war. In early November, a senior Iranian lawmaker said ships from India could pass, and that they would pay a fee. This entry explains why one narrow strip of sea can move petrol and gas prices in Indian homes.
items.hook: Between Iran and Oman lies a strip of sea less than 40 km wide. In normal times, about one in every five barrels of oil the world burns sails through it, and so does much of the cooking gas in Indian kitchens.
